summary: Describes the functional requirements for a routing protocol to run between autonomous systems. It is meant as a precursor to design of a new protocol, covering the DoD IP, ISO IP, and future Internet needs.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC is a set of requirements rather than a protocol. It asks what a routing system between separate networks would have to do: get datagrams to their destination, keep working when part of the network fails, let each network make its own policy decisions, and scale to a very large size. It also says plainly which things it will not try to do, such as congestion control or splitting traffic over several paths.

questions: goals for a new exterior routing protocol
what is inter autonomous system routing
what are the goals of inter as routing
what are the non goals of rfc 1126
subtitle: The 1989 statement of what a routing protocol between networks would have to do.

tldr.problem: Before a new protocol can be designed for routing between separate networks, somebody has to say what it is supposed to achieve, and which of the possible wishes are not going to be met.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC separates an overall set of goals from the functional requirements that follow from them, groups the requirements into areas such as route selection, forwarding and information distribution, and then lists the goals it explicitly abandons.
tldr.outcome: The document was written to be a precursor to a design rather than a design itself, and it says so: it does not specify a standard. Its appendix keeps the earlier, longer discussion of the issues.

today: RFC 1126 was published in October 1989 as a requirements document circulated for comment, and it says of itself that it does not specify a standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated. The protocol it anticipated would be one that spoke between separate networks, and the document was written to be the brief that such a protocol would be checked against.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
The RFC describes the functional requirements for a routing protocol to be used between autonomous systems. It is intended as a necessary precursor to the design of a new inter-autonomous system routing protocol, and specifies requirements for the Internet applicable for use with the current DoD IP, the ISO IP and future Internet protocols. The intention is that these requirements will form the basis for the future development of a new inter-autonomous systems routing architecture and protocol. The document was circulated to the IETF and Internet community for comment, and it states plainly that it does not specify a standard.

The development of such a protocol proceeds from the goals and functions seen as both desirable and obtainable for the Internet environment. The goals indicate properties and general capabilities desired of the Internet routing environment and what the routing architecture is to accomplish as a whole. They are followed by functional requirements, which address either detailed objectives or specific functionality to be achieved by the architecture and the resulting protocols. The requirements are enumerated for clarity and grouped so as to map directly to areas of architectural consideration, and this is followed by a listing and description of general objectives such as robustness that apply in a broad sense. Specific functions which are not reasonably attainable, or are best left to future efforts, are identified as non-requirements.

The intent is to provide the goals and functional requirements in a concise fashion; supporting arguments, trade-off considerations and the like were purposefully omitted, with an appendix addressing that omission to a limited extent. The content is the result of work by the members of the Open Routing Working Group, and the authors intend it to reflect not only what is foreseen in the Internet community but also what is similar to what is encountered in the environments proposed by ANSI, ECMA and ISO.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the shopping list that a future protocol would be checked against. It sets out the goals first, then the things the protocol must actually do, then the things it is allowed to ignore. It is a requirements document, not a proposal.

sections.title: The Overall Goals
sections.content:
In order to derive a set of functional requirements there must be one or more principals or overall goals for the routing environment to satisfy. These high level goals provide the basis for each of the functional requirements and guide the design philosophy for achieving an inter-autonomous system routing solution.

Route to destination. The routing architecture will provide for the routing of datagrams from a single source to one or more destinations in a timely manner. The larger goal is to provide datagram delivery to an identifiable destination, one not necessarily immediately reachable by the source. The concepts of multi-homed hosts and multicast routing services are encompassed by this goal, and datagram delivery is to be provided to all interconnected systems when not otherwise constrained by autonomous considerations.

Routing is assured. Routing services are to be provided with assurance, where the inability to provide a service is communicated under best effort to the requester within an acceptable level of error. This is not to be misconstrued as guaranteed datagram delivery, nor does it imply error notification for every lost datagram; instead, attempts to use network routing services when such a service cannot be provided will result in requester notification within a reasonable period given persistent attempts.

Large system. The design of the architecture, and the protocols within it, should accommodate a large number of routing entities. The exact order of magnitude is a relative guess and the best designs would provide for a practical level of unbounded growth, but the architecture is expected to accommodate the growth of the Internet environment for the next 10 years.

Autonomous operation. The routing architecture is to allow for stable operation when significant portions of the internetworking environment are controlled by disjoint entities. The future Internet environment is envisioned as consisting of a large number of internetworking facilities owned and operated by a variety of funding sources and administrative concerns. Although cooperation between these facilities is necessary to provide interconnectivity, both the degree and the type of cooperation will vary widely, and each facility desires to operate as independently as possible. Those resources used by, and available for, routing are to be allowed autonomous control by the administrative entities which own or operate them, so that each controlling administration should be allowed to establish and maintain policies regarding the use of a given routing resource.

Distributed system. The routing environment developed should not depend upon a data repository or topological entity which is either centralized or ubiquitous. Past experience with a centralized topology has shown that it is both impractical for the needs of the community and restrictive of administrative freedoms. A distributed routing environment should not be restrictive of either redundancy or diversity, and any new routing environment must allow for arbitrary interconnection between internetworks.

Provide a credible environment. The routing environment and services should be based upon mechanisms and information that exhibit both integrity and security. The routing mechanisms should operate in a sound and reliable fashion while the routing information base should provide credible data upon which to base routing decisions. The architecture and protocol designs should be such that the routing environment is reasonably secure from unwanted modification or influence.

Be a managed entity. Provide a manager with insight into the operation of the environment to support resource management, problem solving and fault isolation, allow for management control of the routing system, and collect useful information for the internetwork management environment. Datagram events, and the content and distribution characteristics of relevant databases, are of particular importance.

Minimize required resources. Any feasible design should restrain the demand for resources required to provide inter-autonomous systems routing, of particular interest being those required for data storage, transmission and processing. The design must be practical in terms of today's technology, and specifically must not assume significant upgrades to the existing level of technology in use for data communication systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight goals. Packets must reach their destination; if they cannot, the sender should be told rather than left waiting; the system has to grow to a very large size; each organisation must run its own network as it sees fit without a central authority in the way; the design must be secure enough to trust; it must be manageable; and it must run on the hardware of the day.

sections.title: The Functional Requirements
sections.content:
The functional requirements are derived from the overall goals and describe the critical features expected of inter-autonomous system routing. To an extent these functions are vague in terms of detail: the document does not specify the quantity or types for quality-of-service parameters, which is purposeful, because the requirements are intended to define the features required of the environment rather than the exact nature of it. They are loosely grouped according to areas of architectural impact.

Route synthesis is the area concerned with both route selection and path determination, the identification of a sequence of intermediate systems from a source to a destination. Route synthesis should route around failures dynamically, with a best effort attempt to detect failures in the routing resources currently being used and to use other available resources instead. It should provide loop-free paths: the path from source to destination will be free of circuits or loops most of the time, and when a loop exists it occurs with both negligible probability and duration. It should know when a path or destination is unavailable, both when a path cannot be constructed to a known destination and when the requested destination is unknown. It should provide paths sensitive to administrative policies, though policies dependent upon volatile events of great celerity or which are non-deterministic in nature cannot be accommodated, and paths sensitive to user policies expressed in terms relevant to known characteristics of the topology. It should provide paths which characterise user quality-of-service requirements, using only those resources which can support the desired quality of service, such as bandwidth. And it should provide autonomy between inter- and intra-autonomous system route synthesis: the two environments should operate independently, with neither depending on information from the other for successful functioning.

Forwarding requirements address the datagram forwarding process, which transfers datagrams to intermediate or final destinations based on datagram characteristics, environmental characteristics and route synthesis decisions. The inter-autonomous system forwarding decision should be independent of the intra-autonomous system forwarding decision, although the inter-autonomous delivery process may necessarily depend on intra-autonomous route synthesis and forwarding. Datagrams should not be forwarded when they are deemed administratively inappropriate: policy sensitive route synthesis will prevent normally routed datagrams from using inappropriate resources, but a datagram routed abnormally due to unknown events can always occur, and the only way to prohibit unwanted traffic from entering or leaving an autonomous system is to provide policy enforcement within the forwarding function. A datagram is not to be forwarded to a resource known to be unavailable, notably an intermediate system such as a gateway, which implies some ability to detect and react to resource failures. And the forwarding function is to be sensitive to the characteristics of the datagram: destination, quality of service, precedence, datagram or user policy, and security.

Information requirements cover the nature and disbursal of routing information. The information base must not depend upon either centralization or exact replication, and its content must be sufficient to support all provided routing functionality, with information of particular importance being resource characteristics and resource utilization policies. There must be a means of determining the availability of any utilized resource in a timely manner. The dynamics of routing information flow should be such that a significant portion of transmission resources are not consumed, adjusting to the demands of the environment, the capacities of the distribution facilities used, and the desires of the resource manager. And information distribution is to be sensitive to administrative policies, which may affect the content or completeness of the information distributed, and may determine the extent of it.

Environmental requirements relate to the nature of the environment in which routing is to occur. The routing environment should be capable of supporting datagram transfer within a packet-switched oriented networking environment, and should be designed to accommodate the model for connectionless oriented user transport service. It should accommodate 10K autonomous systems and 100K networks, an order of magnitude that a design which does not accommodate is viewed as inappropriate. And it should allow for arbitrary interconnection of autonomous systems: a practical solution is likely to favour a given structure of interconnectivity for reasons of efficiency, but a design which does not allow for interconnectivity of an arbitrary nature would not be considered feasible.

General objectives are overall objectives for the architecture and its protocols: routing services are to be provided in a timely manner, on a time scale reasonable to support the services provided by the internetwork environment as a whole; autonomous systems or gateways of limited resources should be allowed to participate, even if that participation is not without cost in terms of responsiveness, path optimization or other factors; a design should be sought in which the dissimilarities between autonomous systems do not impinge upon the routing services provided to any autonomous system; the routing environment should accommodate the addressing schemes and protocol mechanisms of autonomous systems, where these may differ among them; and the algorithms and complexities of the design must be such that they can be understood outside of the research community and implementable by people other than the designers themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements fall into five groups. Choosing a path has to cope with failures, avoid loops, respect the policies of the networks involved and honour what the user asked for. Forwarding a packet has to enforce policy at the point of sending, not just when choosing a route. The routing information itself has to be distributed rather than collected in one place, and must not cost more than it is worth. The whole thing has to work over packet-switched links, at a scale of thousands of networks. And it has to be buildable by people outside the research community.

sections.title: The Non-Goals
sections.content:
In view of the conflicting nature of many of the stated goals and the careful considerations and trade-offs necessary to achieve a successful design, it is important to identify those goals or functions which are not being attempted. The following items are not considered to be reasonable goals or functional requirements at this time and are best left to future efforts.

Ubiquity is not a goal: it is not the aim to design a routing environment in which any participating autonomous system can obtain a routing service to any other participating autonomous system in a ubiquitous fashion. Within a policy sensitive routing environment, the cooperation of intermediate resources will be necessary and cannot be guaranteed to all participants, so the concept of ubiquitous connectivity will not be a valid one.

Congestion control is a non-requirement. Additional study is necessary to determine what mechanisms are most appropriate and whether congestion control is best realized within the inter-AS and/or intra-AS environments, and if both, what the dynamics of the interactions between the two are.

Load splitting is a non-requirement: the functional capability to distribute the flow of datagrams from a source to a destination across two or more distinct paths through route synthesis and/or forwarding.

Maximizing the utilization of resources is neither a goal nor a requirement; the environment is not to be designed so that it attempts to maximize the utilization of available resources. Schedule to deadline service is a non-requirement for the inter-autonomous routing environment at this point in time. And non-interference policies of resource utilization are not a requirement: an example of such a policy is one where an autonomous system allows the utilization of excess bandwidth by external users as long as this does not interfere with local usage of the link. The appendix explains the problem with supporting such a policy, the need to be cognizant of highly dynamic state information, and why rapid, persistent and non-deterministic state changes would lead to routing oscillations and looping.
sections.plainLanguage: Some wishes are dropped on purpose. Every network will not be able to reach every other network, because the networks in between have to agree to carry the traffic. Congestion control is left for further study. Traffic will not be spread over several paths. The system will not try to squeeze the most out of every link. And there will be no deadline guarantees.

sections.title: Transitioning to a New Routing Environment
sections.content: Although neither a specific goal nor a functional requirement, consideration must be given to the transition which will occur from the current operational routing environment to a new routing environment. A coordinated effort among all participants of the Internet would be impractical, considering the magnitude of such an undertaking. Particularly, the issues of transitional coexistence, as opposed to phased upgrading between disjoint systems, should be addressed as a means of minimizing the disruption of service. Careful consideration should also be given to any required changes to hosts: it is very unlikely that all hosts could be changed, given historical precedence, their diversity and their large numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Any new routing system has to be introduced while the old one is still running, across an Internet that cannot all be changed at once. The document says plainly that a coordinated switch-over is not practical, so the two have to live side by side for a while.

sections.title: Boundary Gateways and Interior Gateways
sections.content:
The appendix is an edited version of a now defunct document entitled "Requirements for Inter-Autonomous Systems Routing", written by Ross Callon in conjunction with the members of the Open Routing Working Group. The information and discussion in it historically precedes that of the main document and was a major influence on its content, and it is included as a matter of reference.

It defines the terms the rest of the discussion uses. A boundary gateway is any autonomous system gateway which has a network interface directly reachable from another autonomous system. As a member of an autonomous system, it participates in the Interior Gateway Protocol and other protocols used for routing between the gateways of the same autonomous system, and may also participate in an inter-autonomous system routing protocol, interacting with boundary gateways in other autonomous systems either directly or indirectly. An interior gateway is any autonomous system gateway which is not a boundary gateway: it has no network interfaces directly reachable by any other autonomous system, it takes part in the protocols used inside its own autonomous system, and it does not directly exchange routing information with gateways in other autonomous systems. The acronym used for the protocol between boundary gateways is IARP, and the protocol used within an autonomous system is IGP.

From these definitions the appendix sets out architectural issues. The architecture should maximize the independence of the internals of one autonomous system from those of others, which should allow technological and administrative differences among them as well as protection against the propagation of misbehavior. The IARP should not constrain any autonomous system to use any one specific interior protocol. The routing architecture should provide significant flexibility about the interconnection of autonomous systems, and should impose no inherent restriction on interconnection configuration or information passing among them; the restrictions imposed by the core model used by EGP are not acceptable. The appendix also describes routing firewalls, the forms of insulation an autonomous system should have against the rest of the world, including being able to route its own internal traffic in the face of arbitrary failures of other interior protocols and of the inter-AS protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix keeps the long earlier essay. It defines the two kinds of router: a boundary gateway, which has a connection that reaches straight into another network and so talks to that network's routers, and an interior gateway, which does not. The architectural argument is that the protocol between networks should not care what happens inside each one, and should not impose a fixed shape on how the networks are connected to each other.

items.title: Route to destination
items.text: Deliver datagrams from one source to one or more destinations in a timely manner, including to destinations not immediately reachable.

items.title: Routing is assured
items.text: When a service cannot be provided, the requester is told under best effort within a reasonable period. This is not guaranteed delivery.

items.title: Large system
items.text: Accommodate a large number of routing entities, with the growth of the Internet for the next ten years.

items.title: Autonomous operation
items.text: Stable operation when parts of the environment are controlled by disjoint entities, each free to set its own routing policy.

items.title: Distributed system
items.text: No centralized or ubiquitous repository of data or control, so that redundancy and diversity are not restricted.

items.title: A credible environment
items.text: Mechanisms and information with integrity and security, so that routing decisions rest on data worth trusting.

items.title: Be a managed entity
items.text: Insight into the running of the system for resource management, problem solving and fault isolation.

items.title: Minimize required resources
items.text: Restrain the demand for storage, transmission and processing, without assuming upgrades to today's technology.

viz.caption: THE FIVE AREAS OF FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENT

cells: Passing datagrams to intermediate or final destinations.
The nature and disbursal of routing information.
The environment in which routing is to occur.
Overall objectives for the architecture and its protocols.

viz.caption: WHAT THE RFC DELIBERATELY DOES NOT ASK FOR

items.title: Ubiquity
items.text: Not every network will be able to reach every other, because the networks in between must agree to carry the traffic.

items.title: Congestion control
items.text: Left for further study, including whether it belongs in the inter-AS or the intra-AS environment or both.

items.title: Load splitting
items.text: Traffic will not be distributed across two or more distinct paths.

items.title: Maximizing resource use
items.text: The environment is not designed to squeeze the most out of the resources available.

items.title: Schedule to deadline service
items.text: No guarantee that a datagram will arrive by a particular time.

items.title: Non-interference policies
items.text: No policy that lets outside users take spare bandwidth as long as local use is not disturbed; such policies would need highly dynamic state and would cause oscillation.
